body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Four camp talks about Rook's personal story, the Thread of Pilgrimage. The companion is ROOK COLDWAKE (call them Rook in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE FIXED FACTS (the beats in the game's journal; the talks tell these, in Rook's own words, and go no further than they do).
- Rook's Thread: Rook's Pilgrimage. What Rook wants: A headstone for every grave nobody tended, and a plot of his own at the end of the road.
- The Connection already happened in Wickermoor, with Mori Shade, the village undertaker. The journal says: "Mori Shade knew Rook's name before Rook gave it."
- The Discovery, "The Unmarked Rows", happens in the Fields of the Crow (Foxwillow's cornfields). The journal's line for it: "In the Fields of the Crow, Rook found graves nobody had ever counted, and wrote them into his ledger."
- The Confrontation, "The Last Shift", happens in the Crooked Nightmare. The journal's line for it: "In the Crooked Nightmare Rook stood his ground against what he left behind, and wrote the first of the three blank names."
Each talk is had at camp AFTER its chapter is over, so Rook looks back on what happened. You may name the Fields of the Crow (Foxwillow's cornfields) in the Discovery and the Crooked Nightmare in the Confrontation and no other place. Do not describe fights, bosses or villains; Rook speaks of what was found, felt or chosen.

THE INCITEMENT AS IT PLAYED (for the first talk). Rook sometimes misses this scene because Rook is not with the party when it plays in the Parlour of the Crooked House. Then Rook goes back alone, and at camp tells the party what was found. These are the facts of the scene; do not change them, you may add small sensory detail:
[pilgrimage_start]
  NARRATOR: Rain rattles the shutters while pale frost churns inside the crystal ball on the shelf. Tiny faces press hard against the cold glass, mouthin' silent words.
  ROOK: Gross neglect of parish bounds, that is, and three districts without proper stone or seal. Settle down now, we've a docket to clear.
  NARRATOR: The brass knocker on Rook's coffin-lid shield clacks once by itself. He thumbs his scraped badge and flips his damp ledger past grey rubbings to three blank sheets.
  ROOK: Three whole pages left open at the back, and not a decent seal in the valley. No wonder the ground won't hold its quiet.
  the party can say: What are the spirits telling you, Rook?
  the party can say: Hand on the glass. We've got your back.
  the party can say: Leave it. We need a way out.
[pilgrimage_asked]
  NARRATOR: Rook presses a stub of white chalk to the first blank sheet, his cold knuckles steady against the damp leather binding.
  ROOK: Subsidence and unlawful trespass across the parish clay. I've logged the complaint, and we'll see the ground properly cleared before shift's end.
[pilgrimage_steadied]
  NARRATOR: Rook settles a broad palm over the brass knocker on his shield, stoppin' its rattle, and squares his frost-rimmed shoulders beside you.
  ROOK: Good to have proper cover on a night watch. Keep close order and mind the footing, this valley's zoning is a thorough mess.
[pilgrimage_moved_on]
  NARRATOR: Rook slips the chalk into his belt pouch, shuts the soggy ledger with a dull thud, and steps back from the shelf.
  ROOK: Best we keep moving through the damp, then. The masonry in this parlour is draughty enough without us standing idle in the cold.

THE TALKS. Write these four talks, in this order, with these keys.

TALK incitement. Rook tells the party about the Parlour of the Crooked House as one short story at the fire. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 3 or 4 SAY rows (the story, in their own words, ending on a plain statement of how it left them). TWO options only: OPTION 1 asks to hear more or says something that shares the moment; OPTION 2 is the quiet way on, leaving Rook to it. Two replies of 1 NARRATOR row (optional) and 1 or 2 SAY rows. No REASON rows in this talk.

TALK discovery. Rook has come back from the Fields of the Crow (Foxwillow's cornfields) with the Discovery, and wants to tell it. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row to open the scene at the fire, then 6 to 8 SAY rows (one more NARRATOR row is allowed in the middle) that tell what the journal line says in Rook's own words and end on the turn: how it sits with them, with one thing left unsaid. Three options: OPTION 1 asks Rook to say more; OPTION 2 is the answer most like what Rook would want to hear, meeting Rook on Rook's own terms; OPTION 3 is the quiet way on, civil but brisk, brushing it past. Three replies of 1 to 3 rows each, each ending the talk, each with a REASON row. The cool reply (3) must still leave the Discovery told.

TALK confrontation_wait. Rook is at their lowest regard for the party (Strained), and has the Confrontation to tell about the Crooked Nightmare but is holding it back until things are mended. This talk is short. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row and 3 or 4 SAY rows: Rook says there is something to say about it and it will keep, and says, in Rook's own voice, what matters to Rook and that the party's way has drifted from it (do not claim any specific deed the party did). Three options: OPTION 1 listens and owns it (the way to mend); OPTION 2 answers coldly; OPTION 3 says nothing and gives Rook room (this reply has NO REASON row). Replies of 1 or 2 rows. Nothing is lost for good: even the cold reply leaves the door open.

TALK confrontation. Rook's story comes to a head. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 7 to 9 SAY rows (one more NARRATOR row allowed in the middle) that tell what the journal line says in Rook's own words: the heart of their act-three story, plain and a little raw, never grand; Rook may come close to the dark secret and step back; end on the turn and a question or a long silence. Three options: OPTION 1 asks Rook to say more; OPTION 2 is the answer most like what Rook needs to hear; OPTION 3 is the quiet way on, brushing it past. Three replies of 1 to 3 rows each, each ending the talk, each with a REASON row. The cool reply must still leave the Confrontation told.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: incitement, discovery, confrontation_wait, confrontation.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/rook_coldwake-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for ROOK COLDWAKE (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Rook likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/rook_coldwake-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Rook, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK incitement
NARRATOR: Rook sits with his damp ledger open on his knee, thumbin' the scraped brass badge pinned to his coat.
SAY: Stepped back into the Parlour of the Crooked House while the rain was coming down. The crystal ball on the shelf was choked with pale frost instead of smoke.
SAY: Tiny faces pressed up hard against the glass, mouthing complaints with no sound to them, and the brass knocker on my shield gave a sharp clack by itself.
SAY: Flipped my book to the back and found three blank sheets waiting, one for each district in this valley left without proper stone or seal.
SAY: Marked the first complaint down in white chalk, because the dead don't settle when the parish bounds are left in arrears.
OPTION 1: We will help you clear that docket.
OPTION 2: Keep your ledger dry and get some rest.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Rook rests his broad palm flat over the brass knocker on his shield and gives a slow, square nod.
SAY: Good to have proper cover on a night shift. Settle down now, we've got work ahead when the road opens.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Rook slips his stub of chalk into his belt pouch and closes the damp calfskin cover with a soft thud.
SAY: Sound advice in weather like this. I'll keep an eye on the perimeter while the camp is quiet.
TALK discovery
NARRATOR: Rook scrapes dried mud from the rim of his shield with a flat stick, a grey smudge of mason's chalk across his knuckles.
SAY: Walked the back rows in the Fields of the Crow after the noise died down. The soil out in Foxwillow's cornfields was sour and churned to mire.
SAY: Found graves out there that nobody had ever counted, packed in between the roots without a kerb or a boundary stake to mark the lease.
SAY: No names on the stones, no dates in the parish register, just folk left in the wet clay like unfiled paperwork.
NARRATOR: He opens his ledger to a fresh sheet filled with neat, square columns of grey chalk marks.
SAY: Cut temporary markers into the fieldstone where I could and logged every plot into the book by row and pace.
SAY: Mori Shade knew my name before I gave it at her parlour door, and she knew what an honest ledger requires.
SAY: Every soul is owed six feet of level ground and a clean entry on the roll, with my own plot waiting at the end of the road.
SAY: Still have three blank pages at the back that no amount of field tallies seem to fill, though that's an audit for another night.
OPTION 1: Whose names belong on those three blank pages?
OPTION 2: Those graves are on the roll now because of you.
OPTION 3: The tally is done. Pack the ledger away.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Rook runs a thumb along the stiff edge of the back cover, where a red ink blot shows through the lining.
SAY: Folk from an older district where the drainage failed and the timber gave out. When the masonry is plumb, the names will go down in order.
SAY: Best not rush the clerk before the ground is ready.
REASON: You asked about the blank pages at the back of my ledger.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Rook lets out a long, deliberate breath he had forgotten to take, his shoulders droppin' half an inch.
SAY: Obliged for that. A watchman doesn't ask for brass bands, just a clean page and a dry seal.
SAY: Mind the turf by the embers when you turn in.
REASON: You respected the tally I kept for the unmarked graves.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Rook buckles the leather strap around his book and sets it neatly beside his halberd.
SAY: Logged and witnessed, at any rate. The cornfields have their count now, and the shift can move along.
REASON: You kept things brisk after I logged the unmarked graves.
TALK confrontation_wait
NARRATOR: Rook stands near the edge of the firelight with his shield grounded between his boots, the ledger strapped tight under his arm.
SAY: Something came up in the Crooked Nightmare that belongs on the shift log, and I wrote the first of the three blank names down.
SAY: The full report will keep for now, because we've got a wider breach in the parish code to settle first.
SAY: My trade is built on keeping sworn word, respecting the dead, and leaving the stone level where we pass.
SAY: Lately your boots have been drifting across the boundary line, and a warden can't file a clean account when the watch is unruly.
OPTION 1: You are right. We will keep to the code.
OPTION 2: Keep your bylaws to yourself and do your job.
OPTION 3: Say nothing and give him room by the fire.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Rook checks the iron buckle on his shield strap and gives a firm, level nod.
SAY: That's fair phrasing. Let's see how the footing holds on the next stretch, and we'll open the book when the line is straight.
REASON: You owned the drift and promised to keep to the code.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Rook's face goes stiff as cold slate, his hands settlin' square on the rim of his shield.
SAY: I'll keep my post and my halberd in line, never fret. The paperwork stays shut until the conduct improves.
REASON: You told me to keep my bylaws to myself.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Rook turns back toward the dark beyond the wagons, standing quiet at parade rest.
SAY: Best let the embers settle. The night watch is covered.
TALK confrontation
NARRATOR: Rook sits close to the coals with his ledger open to the back, a snapped stub of white chalk resting in his palm.
SAY: Back in the Crooked Nightmare, when the lath and plaster came down, the noise sounded dead ringer for a glacial trench caving in.
SAY: Heard a flat northern voice calling out for a spade under the weight, and my fingers went soft as river mud against the shield.
SAY: Thought for a long count it was the man I left under the ice up in Syndramas, come to audit the badge on my coat.
NARRATOR: He touches the scraped service number on his brass pin, then lays his thumb beside a fresh name written on the first of the three blank sheets.
SAY: Wasn't his voice at all, when I stood my ground and listened past the draught in the flues.
SAY: It was my own voice from the ditch, calling for a shovel I never went back to fetch while another man held the timber.
SAY: Put the first of the three blank names down on the page right there in the dust, in clean block capitals.
SAY: A watchman can square every neglected grave in the parish, and still wonder who is going to sign off on his own plot when the shift ends.
SAY: Suppose you've seen enough rough masonry by now to know when a stone is leaning past regulation.
OPTION 1: Tell me about the man who held the timber.
OPTION 2: You stood your ground this time, and wrote the name.
OPTION 3: The name is in the book now. Get some rest.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Rook folds the corner of the back lining down with a steady grey thumb.
SAY: He was a stonemason's lad with a clean chisel hand, and he kept his post to the end. There are two pages left to fill before his whole file is squared.
SAY: Obliged to you for hearing the first line of it without making a fuss.
REASON: You asked to hear about the man I left under the ice.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Rook takes a slow, square breath for the log, the brass knocker on his shield restin' quiet against his knee.
SAY: Held the line and kept the chalk level, which is a start. Good to know the company on this watch keeps a steady eye on the grade.
SAY: We'll see the other two pages filled properly before the road runs out.
REASON: You told me I stood my ground when I wrote the first name.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Rook shuts the ledger carefully so the fresh chalk won't smear and ties the twine around the binding.
SAY: Entered and filed, and the page is dry. I'll take the first turn by the perimeter while the fire burns down.
REASON: You let the matter rest once the first blank name was logged.
